families.title: Ruler strips
families.mathematics: Each strip’s length is a whole number of units somewhere in its band [lo, hi]. Strips laid end to end from 0 make a join, which ends somewhere in [Σ lo, Σ hi], and every end in between occurs, so one setting outside a window breaks a claim about every join, and the shortest and longest joins together certify a claim nobody can break. Widths add, so the widest band for one strip that keeps every join in a window is the window’s width less the other bands’ widths, pinned at each end by one extreme setting. A strip drawn twice is one strip: in a gap it cancels, so (A + 4) − (A + 1) is exactly 3 while (A + 4) − (B + 1) runs from 1 to 5, and the same A taken away leaves exactly B. A locked total A + B = 12 ties the two strips and can cut a band short. This is interval arithmetic and its dependency problem.
rules: Each strip’s end stays inside its gray band. Strips join end to end from 0, and the ruler shows where a join ends.
A letter drawn twice is one strip: both copies are always the same length.

puzzles.title: Ruler strips playground
puzzles.objective: Set any bands for A and B and try their joins.
puzzles.instruction: Set any bands for A and B and try their joins.
puzzles.controls: Drag the end of a strip or an end of its band, or tap near one. Arrow keys move a focused end.
rules: Each strip’s end stays inside its gray band. Strips join end to end from 0, and the ruler shows where a join ends.
puzzles.idea: Free play with two strips and their bands: where can the join end?
puzzles.prerequisites: None. A partner can set the bands and a claim, and the other tries to break it.
hints: Set the bands, then find the shortest and the longest join.
Make one band wider by one. How much wider does the spread of joins get?
Set both bands to one length each. How many places can the join end?

parent.notice: Whether your child can predict, before dragging, where the shortest and the longest join will end.
parent.prompt: Make a claim like “always reaches 8 and fits within 10” and challenge your child to break it.
parent.explanation: The join ends anywhere from the sum of the left ends to the sum of the right ends, and the spread of joins is as wide as the two bands together.
parent.extension: Ask for the widest band for B that keeps every join inside a window you choose.

puzzles.provenance: Week 51 page 1’s launch (A 2 to 3, B 1 to 2) and Problem 1, made free.

puzzles.title: Two strips
puzzles.objective: Set the strips so the join ends outside 8 to 10, or press Can’t and set the shortest and the longest join.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make the join end outside 8 to 10.
puzzles.instruction: Set the strips so the join ends outside 8 to 10, or press Can’t and set the shortest and the longest join.
puzzles.controls: Drag the end of a strip, or tap its row, to change its length. Arrow keys move a focused end. Press Can’t once you have tried a join, then set the shortest and the longest join.
rules: Each strip’s end stays inside its gray band. Strips join end to end from 0, and the ruler shows where a join ends.
The shaded window is the app’s claim: every join ends inside it.
Can’t says no join ends outside the window. After it, set the shortest and the longest join; a pin keeps each one.
puzzles.idea: One setting outside is enough to break a claim about every setting; the shortest join takes every strip at its shortest.
puzzles.prerequisites: Reading a ruler to 13 and comparing lengths. No adding: the ruler shows where the join ends.
hints: Can the join get out of the window by being too short, or too long?
The shortest join uses the shortest A and the shortest B.
Make A 4 long and B 3 long: the join ends at 7.

parent.notice: Whether your child tries both directions, or reaches for the short end straight away.
parent.prompt: Could a longer join break it?
parent.explanation: The join runs from 4 + 3 = 7 to 6 + 4 = 10, and every end between occurs. Only the shortest setting, ending at 7, is outside 8 to 10: “always reaches 8” fails and “fits within 10” holds.
parent.extension: What is the narrowest window the app could claim that nobody can break? (7 to 10.)

puzzles.provenance: Week 51 K–1 Problem 2 and Grades 2–3 and 4–5 Problem 2: the pair A (4 to 6 units) with B (3 to 4 units), against “always reaches 8 and fits within 10”.

puzzles.title: A long strip
puzzles.objective: Set the strips so the join ends outside 8 to 10, or press Can’t and set the shortest and the longest join.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make the join end outside 8 to 10.
puzzles.instruction: Set the strips so the join ends outside 8 to 10, or press Can’t and set the shortest and the longest join.
puzzles.controls: Drag the end of a strip, or tap its row, to change its length. Arrow keys move a focused end. Press Can’t once you have tried a join, then set the shortest and the longest join.
rules: Each strip’s end stays inside its gray band. Strips join end to end from 0, and the ruler shows where a join ends.
The shaded window is the app’s claim: every join ends inside it.
Can’t says no join ends outside the window. After it, set the shortest and the longest join; a pin keeps each one.
puzzles.idea: The other side of the window: the longest join takes every strip at its longest.
puzzles.prerequisites: Reading a ruler to 13 and comparing lengths. No adding: the ruler shows where the join ends.
hints: Find the shortest and the longest join. Does either get out?
The shortest join ends at 8, inside. The longest uses the longest A and the longest B.
Make A 8 long: the join ends at 11.

parent.notice: Whether your child, after Puzzle 1, tries the short end first and then turns round.
parent.prompt: Which joins get out, and which don’t?
parent.explanation: The join runs from 6 + 2 = 8 to 8 + 4 = 12. It always reaches 8, so the short side holds; the joins ending at 11 or 12 (8 + 3, 7 + 4, 8 + 4) break “fits within 10”.
parent.extension: Narrow the bands so nobody can break the claim. (For example A 6 to 7 and B 2 to 3: joins from 8 to 10.)

puzzles.provenance: Week 51 Grades 2–3 and 4–5 Problem 2 (and K–1 Problem 2): the pair E (6 to 8 units) with F (2 to 4 units), renamed A and B, against the same claim.

puzzles.title: Take A away
puzzles.objective: Make the biggest and the smallest gap.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make the biggest and the smallest gap.
puzzles.instruction: Make the biggest and the smallest gap.
puzzles.controls: Drag the end of a strip, or tap its row, to change its length. Arrow keys move a focused end.
rules: Each strip’s end stays inside its gray band. Strips join end to end from 0, and the ruler shows where a join ends.
A letter drawn twice is one strip: both copies are always the same length.
The gap is between the ends of two rows. A bar below keeps the biggest gap you make and one keeps the smallest.
puzzles.idea: Taking away the very same A leaves exactly B: the gap runs from 3 to 4, not the 1 to 6 that the two rows’ separate ranges suggest.
puzzles.prerequisites: Reading a ruler and comparing two ends. No subtracting: the gap is drawn between the ends.
hints: Which strip changes the gap, and which doesn’t?
Both rows start with the same A, so moving A moves both ends together.
Make B 4 long, then 3 long.

parent.notice: Whether your child drags A, sees the gap stay put, and then turns to B.
parent.prompt: Someone says the gap could be anything from 1 to 6, because the top row ends from 7 to 10 and the bottom from 4 to 6. What is wrong?
parent.explanation: The top row is A + B and the bottom is that same A, so the gap is exactly B: 3 to 4. Using the two ranges separately pairs a long A on top with a short A below, which can’t happen. 1 to 6 is a safe claim but a loose one.
parent.extension: What if the bottom row used a different strip with the same band as A? (Then the gap runs from 1 to 6.)
parent.connection: The dependency problem of interval arithmetic: X + Y − X evaluated piece by piece is wider than Y.

puzzles.provenance: Week 51 Grades 4–5 Problem 9: join A (4 to 6) to B (3 to 4), then remove that very same A; the claimed 1 to 6 is safe but not tightest.

puzzles.title: Two middling strips
puzzles.objective: Set the strips so the join ends outside 8 to 10, or press Can’t and set the shortest and the longest join.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make the join end outside 8 to 10.
puzzles.instruction: Set the strips so the join ends outside 8 to 10, or press Can’t and set the shortest and the longest join.
puzzles.controls: Drag the end of a strip, or tap its row, to change its length. Arrow keys move a focused end. Press Can’t once you have tried a join, then set the shortest and the longest join.
rules: Each strip’s end stays inside its gray band. Strips join end to end from 0, and the ruler shows where a join ends.
The shaded window is the app’s claim: every join ends inside it.
Can’t says no join ends outside the window. After it, set the shortest and the longest join; a pin keeps each one.
puzzles.idea: A claim nobody can break is shown by the two extreme settings: if the shortest and the longest join are inside, every join is.
puzzles.prerequisites: Reading a ruler to 13 and comparing lengths. No adding: the ruler shows where the join ends.
hints: Try the shortest join you can make, then the longest.
With both strips shortest the join ends at 8, and with both longest at 10.
Make A 4 and B 4, press Can’t, then make A 5 and B 5.

parent.notice: Whether your child tries the extremes before pressing Can’t, or presses after one middling join.
parent.prompt: How do you know no join gets out? You haven’t tried them all.
parent.explanation: Every join is at least the two shortest strips, 4 + 4 = 8, and at most the two longest, 5 + 5 = 10. Both are inside 8 to 10, so every join is. The two pinned joins are the whole argument.
parent.extension: Make the window one unit narrower on either side. Which pinned join breaks it?
parent.connection: An interval sum is attained at its endpoints: min (A + B) = min A + min B.

puzzles.provenance: Week 51 Grades 2–3 and 4–5 Problem 2 (and K–1 Problem 2): the pair C (4 to 5) with D (4 to 5), renamed A and B, the only pair that keeps both promises.

puzzles.title: One band to widen
puzzles.objective: Make B’s band as wide as you can while every join ends from 7 to 9, then press Widest and set the shortest and the longest join.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make B’s band as wide as you can while every join ends from 7 to 9.
puzzles.instruction: Make B’s band as wide as you can while every join ends from 7 to 9, then press Widest and set the shortest and the longest join.
puzzles.controls: Drag an end of B’s band, or tap near it. Arrow keys move a focused end. Press Widest, then drag the strips’ ends to the shortest and the longest join.
rules: Each strip’s end stays inside its gray band. Strips join end to end from 0, and the ruler shows where a join ends.
The shaded window is the app’s claim: every join ends inside it.
If some join can end outside the window, the app sets the strips to show one.
Widest says the band can’t grow at either end. After it, set the shortest and the longest join; a pin keeps each one.
puzzles.idea: Each end of the widest band is pinned by one setting: A at 3 forces B to reach 4, and A at 4 stops B past 5.
puzzles.prerequisites: Reading a ruler and the break puzzles. The app does the attacking; the child decides how far each end of the band can go.
hints: Watch the join the app makes. Which end of B’s band lets it out?
With A at 3, B must reach 4; with A at 4, B can be at most 5.
Make B’s band 4 to 5, press Widest, then show 3 + 4 and 4 + 5.

parent.notice: Whether your child shrinks the end that the app’s join escapes through, and then tries to grow each end again.
parent.prompt: Why can’t B’s band be 4 to 6?
parent.explanation: A may be 3 or 4. If B could be 3, then 3 + 3 = 6 falls short of 7; if B could be 6, then 4 + 6 = 10 passes 9. So B’s band is at most 4 to 5, and 4 to 5 works: joins run from 3 + 4 = 7 to 4 + 5 = 9. The window is 2 wide and A’s band is 1 wide, which leaves 1 for B.
parent.extension: If A were exactly 3, how wide could B’s band be? (4 to 6.)
parent.connection: Widths add under interval addition: width(A + B) = width A + width B.

puzzles.provenance: Week 51 Grades 2–3 and 4–5 Problem 3 (A 3 to 4, every join from 7 to 9, the widest card for B), and K–1 Problem 3’s three B cards: the starting band 5 to 6 is its “too long” card.

puzzles.title: One A, then a B
puzzles.objective: Make the biggest and the smallest gap in each pair of rows.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make the biggest and the smallest gap.
puzzles.instruction: Make the biggest and the smallest gap in each pair of rows.
puzzles.controls: Drag the end of a strip, or tap its row, to change its length. Arrow keys move a focused end.
rules: Each strip’s end stays inside its gray band. Strips join end to end from 0, and the ruler shows where a join ends.
A white piece is exactly as long as its number.
A letter drawn twice is one strip: both copies are always the same length.
The gap is between the ends of two rows. A bar below keeps the biggest gap you make and one keeps the smallest.
puzzles.idea: The same A on both rows cancels, so its gap is always 3; a separate B of the same band lets the gap run from 1 to 5, longest less shortest.
puzzles.prerequisites: Reading a ruler and comparing two ends. No subtracting: the gap is drawn between the ends.
hints: Move A and watch both gaps. Which one changes?
The top gap is always 3. The bottom gap is biggest with the longest A and the shortest B.
Make A 6 and B 4 for the biggest bottom gap, then A 4 and B 6 for the smallest.

parent.notice: Whether your child notices that the top gap never moves, and moves A and B opposite ways for the bottom one.
parent.prompt: The bottom strips have the same bands as the top. Why does only the bottom gap change?
parent.explanation: On top, both rows start with the same A, so the ends are A + 4 and A + 1, always 3 apart. Below, A + 4 runs from 8 to 10 and B + 1 from 5 to 7 on its own: the biggest gap is 10 − 5 = 5 and the smallest 8 − 7 = 1.
parent.extension: Can the bottom gap be 3 with A and B different lengths? (No: A + 4 − (B + 1) = 3 needs A = B.)
parent.connection: Dependency in interval arithmetic: (A + 4) − (A + 1) is exactly 3, while [8, 10] − [5, 7] = [1, 5].

puzzles.provenance: Week 51 K–1 Problem 4 and Grades 2–3 and 4–5 Problem 5: the same A twice against a separate B, both 4 to 6, with the white pieces 4 and 1 (the review card’s fix 2: both A’s are always the same).

puzzles.title: Three strips
puzzles.objective: Make C’s band as wide as you can while every join ends from 9 to 14, then press Widest and set the shortest and the longest join.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make C’s band as wide as you can while every join ends from 9 to 14.
puzzles.instruction: Make C’s band as wide as you can while every join ends from 9 to 14, then press Widest and set the shortest and the longest join.
puzzles.controls: Drag an end of B’s band, or tap near it. Arrow keys move a focused end. Press Widest, then drag the strips’ ends to the shortest and the longest join.
rules: Each strip’s end stays inside its gray band. Strips join end to end from 0, and the ruler shows where a join ends.
The shaded window is the app’s claim: every join ends inside it.
If some join can end outside the window, the app sets the strips to show one.
Widest says the band can’t grow at either end. After it, set the shortest and the longest join; a pin keeps each one.
puzzles.idea: Widths add: the window is 5 wide, A’s and B’s bands use 1 and 2, so C’s widest band is 2 wide, pinned by the shortest and the longest join.
puzzles.prerequisites: Reading a ruler and the break puzzles. The app does the attacking; the child decides how far each end of the band can go.
hints: Grow C’s band one end at a time, and watch for a join the app gets out.
The shortest join is 2 + 3 + C’s left end; the longest is 3 + 5 + C’s right end.
Make C’s band 4 to 6, press Widest, then show 2 + 3 + 4 and 3 + 5 + 6.

parent.notice: Whether your child grows each end until the app escapes and then steps back, rather than guessing a band.
parent.prompt: How could you tell the width of C’s band before trying?
parent.explanation: The shortest join is 2 + 3 + c and must reach 9, so C’s left end is at least 4; the longest is 3 + 5 + C’s right end and must fit within 14, so C’s right end is at most 6. C 4 to 6 is the one widest band: its width 2 is the window’s 5 less A’s 1 and B’s 2.
parent.extension: If B’s band were 3 to 6, how wide could C’s band be? (1: from 4 to 5.)
parent.connection: width(A + B + C) = width A + width B + width C, so a target window leaves exactly its width less the others’ for the last band.

puzzles.provenance: New, from Week 51 Problem 3 (the widest card for B) and Grades 2–3 and 4–5 Problem 4 (which strip’s width matters), with a third strip.

puzzles.title: Twelve in all
puzzles.objective: With A + B always 12, make the biggest and the smallest gap between the ends of A and B.
puzzles.visibleObjective: With A + B always 12, make the biggest and the smallest gap.
puzzles.instruction: With A + B always 12, make the biggest and the smallest gap between the ends of A and B.
puzzles.controls: Drag the end of a strip, or tap its row, to change its length. Arrow keys move a focused end.
rules: Each strip’s end stays inside its gray band. Strips join end to end from 0, and the ruler shows where a join ends.
A letter drawn twice is one strip: both copies are always the same length.
The gap is between the ends of two rows. A bar below keeps the biggest gap you make and one keeps the smallest.
A and B always add to 12: their row ends at the wall, and moving one end moves the other.
puzzles.idea: A total locked at 12 ties B to A, cuts A’s band to 7 to 9 (A = 10 would need B = 2), and makes the gap 2A − 12: from 2 to 6.
puzzles.prerequisites: Reading a ruler and comparing two ends. No subtracting: the gap is drawn between the ends.
hints: Drag A as far as it goes each way, and watch B.
A stops at 9, because B can’t be shorter than 3. Then the gap is 9 − 3.
Make A 9 long for the biggest gap, then 7 long for the smallest.

parent.notice: Whether your child notices that A’s end stops before the end of its band, and why.
parent.prompt: A’s band goes up to 10. Why can’t A be 10?
parent.explanation: A + B = 12, so B = 12 − A. B’s band 3 to 7 forces A between 5 and 9, and A’s band 7 to 10 cuts that to 7 to 9. The gap A − B = 2A − 12 runs from 2 (A 7, B 5) to 6 (A 9, B 3). Without the lock the gap could be anything from 0 to 7.
parent.extension: Change the total to 13. Does anything stop A now? (No: A runs over its whole band, 7 to 10, and B is cut to 3 to 6.)
parent.connection: A constraint between variables tightens interval bounds: constraint propagation in interval analysis.

puzzles.provenance: Week 51 Grades 4–5 Problem 8: A 7 to 10, B 3 to 7, their join exactly 12; the smallest and largest gap between their ends.
